symbols.name: r
symbols.role: fresh second-batch allocation fractions after eliminating \(e\)

symbols.name: \mathsf D_{\rho,w}
symbols.def: \mathsf D_{\rho,w}\text{ is the rounded proportional two-batch eliminate-one design}

symbols.name: \widehat h_T
symbols.def: \widehat h_T=\arg\max_{i\ne e}\overline Y_{i,T}^{\mathrm{agg}}\text{ after }\mathsf D_{\rho,w}\text{ eliminates }e

symbols.def: \widehat h_T^{\mathrm{stat}}\text{ is the empirical-best recommendation under the static allocation }w

symbols.name: \mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\mathrm{stat}}

symbols.name: \Gamma_{\rho,w}
symbols.def: \Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)=\lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\rho,w}(\widehat h_T\ne h)\text{ when the limit exists}

symbols.name: \mathcal B_e

symbols.name: N_T
symbols.def: N_T=(N_{i,T}^{(1)},N_{i,T}^{(2)}(e))\text{ is obtained by deterministic largest-remainder rounding of }Tq_i(\rho)\text{ and }Tr_i(e;\rho)

symbols.def: Q_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\text{ is }Q_h^{\mathrm E}\text{ with }q_i\text{ replaced by }N_{i,T}^{(1)}/T

assumptions.condition: For every \(i\in\mathcal A\) and \(t\in\mathbb N\), \(Y_{i,t}\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,s_i)\).
The variables \(\{Y_{i,t}:i\in\mathcal A,\ t\in\mathbb N\}\) are mutually independent.
The vector \(s\) is known before treatment allocation begins.
The set \(\arg\max_{i\in\mathcal A}\mu_i\) is the singleton \(\{h\}\).

definitions.name: Heteroskedastic Gaussian best-arm model
definitions.construction: \mathcal M_K=\{(\mu,s,Y):s\in(0,\infty)^K,\ \mu\in\mathbb R^K,\ Y_{i,t}\sim\mathcal N(\mu_i,s_i)\text{ independently for every }i\in[K],t\in\mathbb N,\text{ and }\arg\max_{i\in[K]}\mu_i\text{ is a singleton}\}.

definitions.name: Variance-aware static equal-gap comparator
definitions.construction: Choose \(w=w^{\mathrm{GNA}}(s)\) by the lexicographically fixed maximin program in the symbol table, assign integer observations by largest-remainder rounding of \(Tw_i\), and deploy the arm with the largest sample mean.

definitions.name: Rounded proportional two-batch eliminate-one design
definitions.construction: Given \((T,s,w,\rho)\), allocate the first \(\lfloor\rho T\rceil\) observations by deterministic largest-remainder rounding of \(w\); eliminate the arm \(e\) with the smallest first-batch sample mean using arm-index tie breaking; allocate every remaining observation among \(i\ne e\) by deterministic largest-remainder rounding of \(w_i/(1-w_e)\); deploy the survivor with the largest aggregate sample mean over both batches, again using arm-index tie breaking.

definitions.name: Finite Gaussian branch programs
definitions.construction: For best elimination use \(Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)=\inf_{x\in\mathcal B_h}\sum_i q_i(\rho)(x_i-\mu_i)^2/(2s_i)\). For each \(e\ne h\) and \(j\ne e,h\), use \(Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)=\inf\{R_e(x,z;\mu):x\in\mathcal B_e,\ m_j(e;x,z)\ge m_h(e;x,z)\}\).

definitions.name: Weighted elimination projection coefficient
definitions.construction: For every possible best arm \(h\), set \(d_{h j}=\sqrt{2(v_h+v_j)}\), \(F_h(t)=t^2/(2v_h)+\sum_{j\ne h}(d_{h j}-t)_+^2/(2v_j)\), \(C_h(v)=\min_{t\ge0}F_h(t)\), and \(C(v)=\min_h C_h(v)\). Compute each \(C_h\) by sorting the \(K-1\) breakpoints \(d_{h j}\), evaluating the clipped stationary point \(t_A=\{\sum_{j\in A}d_{h j}/v_j\}/\{1/v_h+\sum_{j\in A}1/v_j\}\) on each induced interval, and taking the smallest value.

definitions.name: Rounded branchwise Chernoff certificate
definitions.construction: Replace \(q\) and \(r\) in every program of \(\text{def:branch-programs}\) by the exact rounded fractions \(N_{i,T}^{(1)}/T\) and \(N_{i,T}^{(2)}(e)/T\), call the resulting values \(Q_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\) and \(Q_{T,e,j}^{\mathrm T}\), and return \(B_T=\exp\{-TQ_{T,h}^{\mathrm E}\}+\sum_{e\ne h}\sum_{j\ne e,h}\exp\{-TQ_{T,e,j}^{\mathrm T}\}\).

definitions.name: Branch-dual saddle handle for unrestricted two-batch design
definitions.construction: For the variance vector \(s\), optimize the joint finite-branch Gaussian rate over an interior first-batch allocation \(a\in\mathcal W\), a first-batch fraction, and branch-specific interior survivor allocations \(b(e)\), using the dual multipliers of the elimination and terminal polyhedra as a saddle-point certificate over \(\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}\).

statements.statement: Under the variance-aware static comparator, \[\lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log\mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\mathrm{stat}}(\widehat h_T^{\mathrm{stat}}\ne h)=I_w(\mu)=\min_{j\ne h}\frac{\Delta_j^2}{2(v_h+v_j)}.\]
statements.justification: This pins the exact variance-aware benchmark rather than an assumed stand-in.
statements.gap: Kato's GNA-EBA theorem uses this pairwise Gaussian benchmark in the equal-gap maximin regime; the lemma records its full instancewise value for the selected \(w\).
statements.consumer: The static exponent is the denominator used by experiment designers to report the adaptive gain for each fundraising-treatment mean vector.

statements.statement: For every \(0<\rho<1\), the limit defining \(\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)\) exists and equals the finite branch minimum \[\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)=\min\left\{Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu),\ \min_{e\ne h}\min_{j\ne e,h}Q_{e,j}^{\mathrm T}(\rho,\mu)\right\}.\] Each infimum over a closed branch polyhedron equals the infimum over its strict-interior error event, and replacing ideal proportions by the largest-remainder counts \(N_T\) leaves this limit unchanged.
statements.justification: Exact equality, rather than a one-sided concentration exponent, is necessary for an optimality frontier.
statements.gap: Imbens, Qin, and Wager are the closest same-design comparator: under a common Gaussian variance, their batched arm-elimination result gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation, but it does not establish a heteroskedastic exact branch formula. The first changed steps are the weighted Gaussian contraction of each elimination branch and exact equality for the coupled terminal branches that reuse first-batch observations, including strict-interior attainment and rounding invariance.
statements.consumer: The equality gives ranking-and-selection software a finite list of convex programs that exactly diagnose whether elimination or final comparison drives asymptotic error.

statements.statement: For each \(h\in\mathcal A\), \(C_h(v)>1\), and \[Q_h^{\mathrm E}(\rho,\mu)\ge\rho C_h(v)I_w(\mu).\] Equality holds at the normalized witness \(\mu_h=0\) and \(\mu_j=-d_{h j}\) for all \(j\ne h\). Moreover, the active-set construction in \(\text{def:projection-coefficient}\) evaluates \(C_h\) after at most \(K\) one-dimensional quadratic pieces.
statements.justification: The strict weighted projection coefficient is the source of improvement for every positive variance profile.
statements.gap: Imbens, Qin, and Wager obtain the common-variance coefficient \((K-1)/K\) inside their information lower bound; the heteroskedastic coefficient and its exact equality witness are new.
statements.consumer: The one-dimensional computation lets an experimental platform calculate a certified gain from its arm-specific historical variances.

statements.statement: For every positive finite variance vector \(s\) and every unique-best \(\mu\), one has \(1/C<\rho^\star<1\), and the design \(\mathsf D_{\rho^\star,w}\) satisfies \[\Gamma_{\rho^\star,w}(\mu)\ge G I_w(\mu)>I_w(\mu),\qquad G=\frac{C(1+\eta)}{C+\eta}>1.\] Thus proportional late elimination strictly improves the instancewise error exponent of Kato's variance-aware static equal-gap maximin allocation throughout \((0,\infty)^K\).
statements.justification: This is the theorem-level kernel: heterogeneity never creates a positive-variance exception to late-elimination admissibility.
statements.gap: Imbens, Qin, and Wager prove common-variance dominance over uniform allocation, while Kato proves equal-gap maximin optimality of a static heteroskedastic allocation; neither proves this strict cross-result dominance.
statements.consumer: A multi-arm fundraising experiment with known outcome variances can replace its generalized-Neyman static schedule by the stated two-batch schedule without sacrificing any fixed unique-best instance asymptotically.

statements.statement: For every \(0<\rho<1\), the exact worst-instance multiplier within \(\mathfrak D_2\) is \[\inf_{\mu:\,|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}\frac{\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}=\min\left\{\rho C,\ 1+(1-\rho)\eta\right\}.\] A best-elimination witness with \(h\in\arg\min_k C_k\) attains the first branch. For an \(e\in\arg\min_k w_k/(1-w_k)\), two distinct survivors and a sufficiently separated eliminated arm attain the second branch. Consequently \(\rho^\star\) uniquely maximizes the displayed value and the maximum is \(G\).
statements.justification: Matching branch witnesses certify optimal timing rather than merely proposing a favorable first-batch fraction.
statements.gap: Existing batched results optimize fixed-confidence sample or batch complexity, and existing adaptive large-deviation results give bounds; none evaluates this constrained heteroskedastic fixed-budget saddle value.
statements.consumer: The theorem supplies a tuning rule that is minimax within the implementable proportional family and identifies which stress-test instance limits it.

statements.statement: For \(K=3\) and \(s=(1,1,4)\), the static selector is \[w_1=w_2=\frac{\sqrt2-1}{2},\qquad w_3=2-\sqrt2.\] The active coefficient is \(C=C_3=(6+2\sqrt2)/7\), \(\eta=(2\sqrt2-1)/7\), \(\rho^\star=2\sqrt2-2\), and \(G=(8\sqrt2-4)/7\). The best-arm-elimination witness with \(h=3\) has exponent \(G I_w\), and the terminal witness eliminating arm \(1\) with survivors \(2,3\) also has exponent \(G I_w\).
statements.justification: Exact radicals make the early numerical stress test reproducible and destructive if the branch coupling is wrong.
statements.gap: No cited source analyzes this heteroskedastic three-arm design; the proposition verifies the most delicate variance profile used to audit the general formula.
statements.consumer: Implementers obtain a fixed regression test with \(G\approx1.044815499855\) for quadratic-program and rounding code.

statements.statement: For every budget large enough that each prescribed positive count is at least one, \[\mathbb P_{\mu,s}^{\rho,w}(\widehat h_T\ne h)\le B_T(\mu,s,\rho,w).\] The certificate contains one best-elimination term and exactly \((K-1)(K-2)\) terminal branch terms, uses the implemented integer counts without asymptotic replacement, and satisfies \[\lim_{T\to\infty}-T^{-1}\log B_T(\mu,s,\rho,w)=\Gamma_{\rho,w}(\mu).\]
statements.justification: The same branch geometry should yield a conservative finite-budget deliverable without hiding rounding in asymptotic notation.
statements.gap: Lalitha et al. give stagewise heterogeneous-variance bounds for SHVar; this certificate instead retains the exact coupled late-elimination branch programs and their limiting exponent.
statements.consumer: The published \(\texttt{bbandits}\) successive-elimination workflow can expose \(B_T\) as a pre-deployment error certificate for a chosen integer fundraising budget.

statements.statement: If \(s_i=\sigma^2\) for every arm, then \(w_i=1/K\), \(C=2(K-1)/K\), \(\eta=1/(K-1)\), \[\rho^\star=\frac{K^2}{2(K-1)^2+K},\qquad G=\frac{2K(K-1)}{2(K-1)^2+K}.\] In particular, \(K=3\) gives \(\rho^\star=9/11\) and \(G=12/11\), recovering the common-variance late-elimination improvement.
statements.justification: This mandatory reduction checks the weighted formula against the known symmetric geometry.
statements.gap: Imbens, Qin, and Wager establish common-variance dominance; the proposition shows that the new weighted theorem contains that regime rather than replacing it by an analogue on a disjoint class.
statements.consumer: Readers can benchmark the heteroskedastic schedule against the familiar equal-allocation design and reproduce the three-arm gain by hand.

statements.statement: Using the branch-dual saddle handle in \(\text{def:full-class-handle}\), characterize \[\sup_{D\in\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}}\inf_{\mu:\,|\arg\max_i\mu_i|=1}\frac{\Gamma_D(\mu)}{I_w(\mu)}.\] Is its value \(G\), so that the proportional schedule is already optimal, or can a nonproportional first-stage or survivor allocation achieve a strictly larger certified multiplier? Derive an attaining design and a matching saddle certificate in either case.
statements.justification: The unrestricted two-batch design frontier is the genuine open content beyond the exact proportional-family theorem.
statements.gap: Jun et al. and Jin et al. study batch constraints under different fixed-budget or fixed-confidence criteria; no cited theorem gives this heteroskedastic robust-gain saddle value.
statements.consumer: A solution determines whether experimental platforms lose any worst-instance exponent by enforcing the simple proportional survivor-allocation interface.

sampling_model.design: A fixed-budget two-batch rule assigns the first fraction \(\rho\) according to known variance-only weights \(w\), eliminates the lowest first-batch empirical mean, and assigns the rest proportionally among survivors.
sampling_model.units: For each arm, experimental outcomes are independent Gaussian draws with a fixed unknown mean and a known finite positive arm-specific variance.
sampling_model.treatment: There are \(K\ge3\) mutually exclusive treatment arms, and exactly one treatment is assigned to each sampled unit.
sampling_model.overlap: Every arm receives a positive first-batch fraction, and every survivor receives a positive second-batch fraction.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no nuisance estimation in the selected kernel because the variance vector is known; unknown-variance adaptation remains outside scope.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: Their sufficient-condition theorem gives strict large-deviation dominance of batched elimination over uniform allocation under a common Gaussian variance.
The GNA-EBA allocation maximizes the worst equal-gap Gaussian exponent using known heterogeneous variances.
An upper large-deviation bound for adaptive sampling proportions transfers to an upper bound for empirical rewards.
SHVar has a finite-budget exponential upper bound under known heterogeneous reward variances.
No fixed-budget algorithm uniformly matches the stronger mean-aware static-oracle exponent for \(K\ge3\) in a regular one-parameter natural exponential family.
Three batches attain asymptotically optimal fixed-confidence sample complexity.

tldr: For any \(K\ge3\) and any known finite positive Gaussian variance vector, the variance-aware static equal-gap maximin allocation is strictly dominated, at every unique-best mean vector, by a fully specified proportional two-batch rule that eliminates the lowest first-batch arm and reallocates its remaining share among survivors. The closest same-design result is Imbens, Qin, and Wager’s common-variance batched-elimination dominance theorem; the first changed steps are a heteroskedastic weighted contraction and an exact terminal-branch equality for the coupled two-batch error event. These steps yield the exact finite-branch exponent, a one-dimensional weighted projection coefficient \(C>1\), and matching elimination and terminal witnesses showing that \(\rho^\star=(1+\eta)/(C+\eta)\) delivers the exact proportional-family gain \(G=C(1+\eta)/(C+\eta)>1\). A rounded branchwise Chernoff certificate connects the exponent calculation to finite experimental budgets.

project_justification.gap: The closest same-design result, Imbens, Qin, and Wager’s common-variance batched arm-elimination theorem, gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. It does not supply the heteroskedastic weighted branch contraction, exact terminal-branch equality, or dominance over Kato’s variance-aware equal-gap maximin allocation.
project_justification.niche: The proportional eliminate-one family preserves the batched-elimination design studied by Imbens, Qin, and Wager while making known arm-specific variances enter every elimination and terminal contraction, so the effect of heterogeneity can be isolated without changing the design motif.
project_justification.fill: The project derives the weighted heteroskedastic contraction and exact coupled terminal-branch equality, then reduces the worst best-elimination event to \(K\) one-dimensional piecewise-quadratic calculations, proves a whole-positive-orthant gain, and certifies the exact maximin timing within the proportional family.

related_work: Imbens, Qin, and Wager are the closest same-design comparator: under a common Gaussian variance, their batched arm-elimination result gives sufficient conditions for strict large-deviation dominance over uniform allocation. The first changed steps here are the heteroskedastic weighted contraction of the elimination branches and exact equality for the coupled terminal branches; these steps also permit the comparator to change from uniform allocation to Kato’s generalized Neyman allocation. Kato derives that variance-aware comparator from a worst equal-gap Gaussian experiment, without asserting its pointwise admissibility away from equal gaps. Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere provide an adaptive large-deviation upper-bound technique, while their explicit completeness caveat leaves room for the finite-branch equality proved here. Lalitha et al. show how known heterogeneous variances should alter elimination allocations and provide finite-budget bounds; their stagewise analysis informs the supporting certificate but is not used as an exact exponent comparator. Goldberger rules out universal matching of the stronger mean-aware static oracle, which is consistent with this paper because \(w\) depends only on variances and is deliberately weaker. Jin et al. optimize a fixed-confidence batched criterion, whereas this paper solves an exact fixed-budget robust-gain game in a two-batch subclass.
technical_internal_limitation: The finite-budget quantity \(B_T\) is an upper certificate for the adaptive design's error probability. Comparing it with another upper certificate does not by itself prove finite-sample risk dominance. The theorem-level dominance claim is therefore confined to exact large-deviation exponents.
honest_scope: The exact finite-branch equality, weighted projection inequality, whole-positive-orthant dominance, and matching proportional-family witnesses are all proof obligations. The early exact-algebra check at \(s=(1,1,4)\) supports rather than proves the general theorem. Optimality in \(\mathfrak D_2^{\mathrm{all}}\), unknown-variance adaptation, non-Gaussian outcomes, variance ratios changing with \(T\), and finite-sample risk dominance remain open. The equal-variance proposition and the failure of strict gain at \(K=2\) are required reductions.

seed_details.seed: Exact finite-branch large deviations for a proportional two-batch eliminate-one rule
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, Theorem 1, its proof, and the Conclusion. Theorem 1 transfers an upper large-deviation bound for empirical allocation proportions to an upper bound for empirical rewards; the authors explicitly state that it is not a complete large-deviation principle and list completeness as future work.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to replace the allocation-proportion upper bound by a direct finite-mixture contraction over the first-batch elimination cones and the fresh second-batch Gaussian means. Open and closed cone infima, reuse of the first batch, and integer rounding then have to be handled jointly.
seed_details.destination_search: A focused search for \(\text{two-batch}\), \(\text{heteroskedastic Gaussian}\), \(\text{exact error exponent}\), and \(\text{eliminate one}\) found Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere's upper-bound transfer and Imbens, Qin, and Wager's common-variance lower bound, but no exact heteroskedastic branch equality.
seed_details.novelty_check: The candidate survives: the closest adaptive large-deviation theorem supplies only the closed-set direction, the common-variance paper supplies only a lower exponent bound, and the Gaussian change-of-measure paper treats exact matching primarily for two arms.
seed_details.red_team: Immediate from Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere because their Theorem 1 already contracts adaptive allocations and rewards.
seed_details.rebuttal: Their theorem gives only a large-deviation upper bound and expressly does not give the lower bound needed for equality; the finite branch structure supplies the missing interior-attainment argument.

seed_details.seed: Universal heteroskedastic dominance over the generalized-Neyman static design
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, the best-arm worst-case lower bound, the GNA-EBA upper bound and equal-gap optimality theorem, and the Conclusion. The comparator is the variance-only allocation \(w^{\mathrm{GNA}}\) maximizing the worst equal-gap Gaussian exponent; its theorem does not claim pointwise optimality away from equal gaps.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is Kato's static pairwise Gaussian projection: add a late eliminate-one branch and solve the weighted projection for the event that the true best arm is the first-batch loser. The new coefficient \(C_h\) must be strictly larger than one for every positive variance vector.
seed_details.destination_search: The target--method search combined generalized Neyman allocation with two-batch elimination, heteroskedastic dominance, and admissibility. It found Imbens, Qin, and Wager only under common variance and Lalitha et al. only with concentration bounds, not the claimed all-positive-variance comparison.
seed_details.novelty_check: The candidate survives: no adjacent source compares late elimination with Kato's variance-only allocation on every unique-best mean cone, and Goldberger's impossibility concerns the strictly stronger mean-aware oracle.
seed_details.red_team: Immediate from Imbens, Qin, and Wager because their two-batch rule universally dominates completely randomized trials.
seed_details.rebuttal: Their maintained model has a common Gaussian variance and uniform allocation; the weighted projection, the generalized-Neyman comparator, and strict dominance over every positive heteroskedastic variance vector are absent.

seed_details.seed: Exact robust-gain frontier inside the proportional two-batch family
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at its adaptive large-deviation theorem, the Successive Rejects theorem, the construction sections, and the Conclusion. Its algorithms improve exponent lower bounds, but it does not solve the max--min game within a proportional two-batch subclass.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to turn a one-sided branch lower bound into matching least-favorable best-elimination and terminal-misranking witnesses, and then balance their affine functions of the first-batch fraction.
seed_details.destination_search: Searches pairing proportional two-batch sampling with exact minimax multiplier found fixed-confidence batch-complexity results and general fixed-budget minimax games, but no closed-form constrained-family saddle value.
seed_details.novelty_check: The candidate survives: adjacent batched papers optimize different criteria, the global minimax construction does not evaluate this proportional subclass, and the stronger-oracle impossibility leaves the weaker benchmark game available.
seed_details.red_team: The multiplier is a trivial optimization after obtaining the lower bound.
seed_details.rebuttal: Balancing two lower bounds is trivial, but proving equality requires separate coupled Gaussian witnesses that attain both branches for arbitrary positive weights and variances; this is the load-bearing frontier result.

seed_details.seed: A rounded finite-budget Gaussian Chernoff certificate
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, the SHVar allocation lemma, the known-variance error theorem, and the Conclusions. Its proof combines deterministic pull-count control with pairwise sub-Gaussian tails and a stagewise union bound.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to replace stagewise pair tails by Mahalanobis projections of the feasible elimination-and-terminal polyhedra, while retaining exact integer counts.
seed_details.destination_search: Searches for rounded two-batch Gaussian branch certificates found SHVar's finite-budget bounds and Successive Rejects bounds, but not a certificate whose exponential term is the exact late-elimination quadratic program.
seed_details.red_team: This is only a union bound with Gaussian tails.
seed_details.rebuttal: The supporting-hyperplane step is standard, but the coupled branch polyhedra and exact rounded count coefficients make the certificate operational; it is retained as a supporting result rather than the kernel.

seed_details.seed: Necessary and sufficient pilot growth for unknown-variance oracle exponents
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the SHAdaVar construction, the Gaussian variance concentration lemma, the unknown-variance error theorem, and the Conclusions. SHAdaVar controls underestimation through optimistic variance bounds but does not identify the fixed-budget oracle exponent.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to replace high-probability variance control by a joint large-deviation principle for pilot sample means and variances, because exponentially rare variance underestimation can control the final error rate.
seed_details.destination_search: Jourdan, Degenne, and Kaufmann's fixed-confidence unknown-variance transportation costs and Kato's pilot-plus-screening simple-regret results occupy adjacent criteria, not fixed-gap probability-of-error exponents.
seed_details.red_team: A logarithmic pilot consistently estimates each variance and therefore preserves the oracle rule.
seed_details.rebuttal: Consistency is insufficient on the \(T\)-scale: a logarithmic pilot has only polynomially small severe-underestimation probability, which can overwhelm an exponentially small recommendation error.

seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, the asymptotic sample-complexity, correctness, and batch-complexity theorems, and the Conclusion. Three batches attain fixed-confidence asymptotic complexity, but the results do not evaluate exact fixed-budget heteroskedastic exponents for eliminating several arms at once.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to replace the fixed-confidence tracking event by a weighted projection onto an order-statistic cone in which the best arm falls below \(m\) competitors.
seed_details.destination_search: The target--method search located batch-constrained fixed-confidence procedures and common-variance batched elimination, but not the heteroskedastic fixed-budget eliminate-\(m\) dominance boundary.
seed_details.red_team: This is a routine \(m=1\) to general-\(m\) extension.
seed_details.rebuttal: The active order-statistic cone changes combinatorially with the variance profile and the terminal survivor set; nevertheless this breadth makes it a less focused first version than eliminate one.

seed_details.seed: Top-\(m\) proportional elimination with exact weighted projections
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at its Conclusion, which names top-\(m\) identification as a destination, and at Theorem 1, whose allocation-to-reward upper-bound transfer is the proposed method ancestor.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to contract the joint Gaussian branch law onto a set-valued ranking error rather than the single-best misranking cone.
seed_details.destination_search: Searches pairing top-\(m\) identification with heteroskedastic two-batch exact exponents found successive accept-and-reject guarantees, not a universal dominance theorem over a variance-only static benchmark.
seed_details.red_team: The top-\(m\) result follows by replacing one union over challengers with another.
seed_details.rebuttal: Elimination and terminal mistakes become coupled set-selection cones, but no evidence yet shows a strict coefficient larger than one for every variance vector; the seed is dropped rather than padded.

seed_details.seed: Local non-Gaussian transfer of the dominance gain
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, the Gaussian impossibility theorem, the local quadratic Kullback--Leibler lemma, the natural-exponential-family theorem, and the Discussion. Its local quadratic transfer establishes an impossibility relative to the mean-aware static oracle, not positive dominance over a variance-only comparator.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to transfer the weighted projection inequality through uniform local Kullback--Leibler expansions while keeping the adaptive branch deviations inside the local neighborhood.
seed_details.destination_search: No paper located in the focused search transfers the common-variance admissibility theorem to heterogeneous regular natural exponential families with a quantitative positive gain.
seed_details.red_team: Goldberger's local quadratic lemma makes the extension automatic.
seed_details.rebuttal: The lemma controls local alternatives only, whereas universal instancewise dominance requires global control of every branch rate; no such global inequality is presently justified.

seed_details.seed: A scalable certificate for multi-stage variance-aware successive elimination
seed_details.anchor_read: The arXiv source was opened at the Introduction, its minimax fixed-budget optimization and attaining delayed-tracking construction, and the Conclusion. The exact minimax construction is computationally prohibitive, and scalability is left open.
seed_details.proof_boundary: The first changed step is to replace the global instance--allocation game by successive finite branch projections with a computable approximation-ratio certificate.
seed_details.destination_search: The search found neural approximations and stagewise concentration bounds, but no observable certificate that bounds the exponent loss of a scalable heteroskedastic successive-elimination schedule.
seed_details.red_team: This is an engineering approximation to an existing minimax program.
seed_details.rebuttal: A certified approximation ratio would be theorem-level, but the current substrate does not yet yield a nontrivial ratio, so the seed is not selected.

literature_map.settled: For common known Gaussian variance and \(K\ge 3\), simple batched arm-elimination designs satisfy sufficient conditions for strict instancewise dominance over uniform allocation.
literature_map.open_here: The published theorem does not cover arbitrary positive heterogeneous variances, a variance-aware static comparator, or the exact robust multiplier of the proportional two-batch rule.

literature_map.settled: Generalized Neyman allocation is maximin in Kato's equal-gap Gaussian regime, while SHVar and SHAdaVar have finite-budget error upper bounds based on variance-proportional sampling.
literature_map.open_here: Neither source gives a strict pointwise adaptive improvement over the variance-only maximin allocation or an exact coupled branch exponent.

literature_map.settled: Adaptive allocation upper large-deviation bounds can be transferred to empirical rewards, and Gaussian two-arm alternatives yield exact change-of-measure benchmarks.
literature_map.open_here: A matching lower large-deviation bound for the data-selected elimination branch and its aggregate terminal comparison remains absent.

literature_map.settled: Three batches suffice for fixed-confidence asymptotic optimality; a fixed-budget minimax exponent game has a computationally difficult attaining rule; no algorithm uniformly matches the stronger mean-aware static oracle for \(K\ge3\).
literature_map.open_here: These results do not preclude dominance over Kato's weaker variance-only equal-gap benchmark and do not solve the exact proportional two-batch constrained game.

literature_map.settled: Unknown-variance Gaussian fixed-confidence procedures and pilot-based simple-regret procedures can estimate variances adaptively.
literature_map.open_here: They use different criteria and do not determine the fixed-gap probability-of-error exponent of the known-variance proportional rule; this extension is outside the selected core.

literature_checklist.author: Imbens, Qin, and Wager
literature_checklist.one_line: Common-variance batched arm elimination strictly dominates uniform allocation under a sufficient batch-weight condition.

literature_checklist.author: Kato
literature_checklist.one_line: Generalized Neyman allocation is maximin for the known-variance equal-gap Gaussian regime.

literature_checklist.author: Wang, Tzeng, and Proutiere
literature_checklist.one_line: An allocation-proportion large-deviation upper bound transfers to empirical rewards, without a complete adaptive large-deviation principle.

literature_checklist.author: Lalitha, Kalantari, Ma, Deoras, and Kveton
literature_checklist.one_line: SHVar and SHAdaVar give heterogeneous-variance elimination rules and finite-budget error bounds.

literature_checklist.author: Kaufmann, Cappe, and Garivier
literature_checklist.one_line: Change of measure yields best-arm lower bounds and exact two-arm Gaussian allocations.

literature_checklist.author: Jin, Yang, Tang, Xiao, and Xu
literature_checklist.one_line: Three batches suffice for fixed-confidence asymptotic sample-complexity optimality.

literature_checklist.author: Goldberger
literature_checklist.one_line: No algorithm uniformly attains the mean-aware static-oracle exponent when \(K\ge3\) in regular one-parameter natural exponential families.

literature_checklist.author: Qin
literature_checklist.one_line: Instance-dependent fixed-budget complexity and uniform dominance are posed as central open problems.
